inline.s: Before the conversation was finished, Wang Jueru suddenly woke up. Opening his eyes and recalling, he felt that Layman Zhu's speech and bearing, radiant and full of auspicious marks, stood vividly before his eyes — utterly unlike any inverted dream. He rose and looked at the clock; it was just past five in the afternoon. A month later, with winter ended and spring returned, Wang Jueru chanced to meet Wang Nengzhi, a relative by marriage of Layman Zhu. The moment they met, Wang Nengzhi said to Wang Jueru in haste: “How strange! Last winter Zhu Xingwu came to talk with me several times, saying that he had already been reborn in the borderland of the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss and had come specially to report. I have long wished to visit you and tell you all this.” Wang Jueru eagerly asked what Layman Zhu had said. Wang Nengzhi related: “The moment I saw him, I asked, ‘Where have you been these past few months, and why did you not come back sooner to report?’ Layman Zhu replied, ‘I was detained for a long while in the underworld on a certain matter. It was only by the grace of Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva, who sent someone to escort me, that I could steal the time to come.’ He went on, ‘When I was alive, I gave you books on Buddha-recitation — have you practiced in accordance with them? In the past you ran a restaurant and slaughtered many creatures; your offenses are extremely heavy. From now on, besides striving in Buddha-recitation, you must all the more repent, and you must take up a vegetarian diet and strictly abstain from killing. Rebirth in the West is a share for every person, and it is very easy — by no means give up on yourself. I very much regret that I took up Buddha-recitation too late and that my practice was too poor; you ought to enter into practice as early as possible, as the essential thing.’ And so on.” After Layman Zhu had reported back, Wang Jueru's friends, hearing of this, all urged him to write it out and publish it, to awaken people's faith. Wang Jueru therefore wrote it plainly according to the facts, and appended to the manuscript a note: “I solemnly make this vow by the precepts: there is not a single false word, nor have I added or subtracted so much as one word of Layman Zhu's replies in the dream.” Yesterday he sent it by special letter to this journal, requesting its publication. We now publish his account to inform the monastic and lay community of the whole land.
Original text:

Layman Zhu Dingyi, courtesy name Jingchen, also known by the courtesy name Xingwu, was a man of Kunming in Yunnan. He practiced medicine, and in his leisure often cultivated the method of quiet sitting.

, on the advice of his close friend Layman Wang Jueru, he changed to the practice of the Buddha-recitation Dharma gate and was quite diligent. The following summer he happened to catch a cold and lay weary in bed. Wang went to visit him and urged him to go to the outskirts of the city
(the suburbs)

, the renowned Yunqi Monastery, to rest and recover while listening to the lectures on the Śūraṅgama Sūtra, and accompanied him there. Returning after ten days, Wang visited again and found him suffering from diarrhea as well. He urged him, saying: You are a physician and can diagnose and treat yourself, but now that the illness has come to this, I fear your understanding and judgment may be wanting in accuracy; why not summon another physician for a consultation, so that you may recover sooner? The layman said: No, no. After you went to hear the sutra, there was one night when I saw Amitābha Buddha in a dream, and I joyfully made obeisance. Just as I was prostrating with the five limbs to the ground, I saw the Great One in White, his body likewise tall, coming toward me face to face. As he drew near, fearing his robe might brush against me, he lifted the hem with his hand and floated gently past my side, his smile brimming with warmth. Observing his manner, he seemed about to receive me and lead me to the West; what need is there to summon another physician for a further diagnosis? Before long the illness grew worse; knowing his time had come, he entrusted Wang with inviting a bhikshu to his home to assist in recitation, and thus on the night of the sixth day of the sixth month, he passed away seated in lotus, reciting the Buddha's name.
[Lift the hem (kōu yī)] To lift up the hem of the robe.

When Wang, on his behalf, invited the bhikshu to come and recite the Buddha's name, the layman said of himself: I will surely depart tonight. Wang, half-doubting and half-believing, made an agreement with him, saying: At present, rebirth in the West through Buddha-recitation is attested only by the auspicious signs at death; after rebirth in the West there is no other conclusive proof. If you attain rebirth in the West this time, you must come in person to report and prove the truth of it; remember this most earnestly. The layman said: How shall I report? Wang said: Have you not seen the record in the books of Que Gongze's reporting after rebirth in the West? The layman said: That manner of reporting requires nothing less than the highest grade of the highest birth; how could I do it? I can only report through a dream. Wang said: That is fine too, so long as it proves it.

[Que Gongze] The Biographies of Laymen says: “Que Gongze was a man of Zhao. In the reign of Emperor Wu of the Jin dynasty he lived in Luoyang, aloof, serene, and untrammeled, and every day recited the Zhengfa Hua Sutra. After he passed away, his friends held an assembly for him at the White Horse Monastery, and in the evening they turned the sutra. Suddenly a voice was heard in the air; looking up, they beheld a man whose form and color were bright and beautiful, who said: ‘I am Que Gongze. I have been born in the Western Land of Bliss and have come with all the superior ones to hear the sutra.’ All in the hall saw him together. There was a man of Ji Commandery named Wei Shidu, who had studied under Gongze; his mother often offered food to the monks. That day, near noon, a bowl suddenly descended from the air and landed directly before the mother. On close inspection, it was the very bowl Gongze had always used, filled with rice, its fragrance filling the hall, and those who ate of it were not hungry for seven days.” Zhi Daolin composed a praise for him: “Great is Lord Que, who drank the void and took in spirit; his spirit wrought wonders in the West, his traces answered in the East; he lingers amid the vaults of heaven, his fame resounding, his form resplendent — would he begrudge this single praise, or not reveal himself beyond the dark?” [Superior ones] Men of superior virtue, an honorific for bhikshus, because a bhikshu holds virtue and wisdom within and has surpassing conduct without, standing above other men. [Zhi Daolin] (
) was an eminent monk of the Jin dynasty. His name was Dun, but he was known by his courtesy name. He was a native of Kaifeng. At the age of

he left home, and was friends with Xie An, Wang Xizhi, and others, delighting in the discussion of abstruse principles. He wrote the Treatise on Form-as-Such Roaming in the Mysterious, in which he propagated
form-as-such is empty
, developing the prajñā teaching of the emptiness of nature; he was one of the six great masters of prajñā studies.

After he passed away seated, in accordance with the Buddha's rule he was placed in the coffin and cremated, and his ashes placed in a stupa. When all was done, it was already mid-June. Time flew like a galloping colt; in the blink of an eye July, August, and September had passed, and there was no news at all. I secretly thought that the layman had not attained rebirth in the West, or that, having attained it, he was unwilling to communicate with us, so that the agreement could not be fulfilled. But
(unexpectedly)
on the last day of the eleventh month
(the end of the eleventh lunar month)

, one day, Wang, suffering from a toothache, lay resting in bed in broad daylight. In a daze, he saw the layman ascend the stairs and sit on a stool. (Original note: Because Wang recited the Buddha's name, his bed was placed beside the Buddha hall upstairs.) His build was as before; he wore a half-new flat cap and clothes that seemed recently washed, all clean, with a radiance shining in. His expression was bright and lively, his face like a full moon, and his skin delicate and tender like a handsome boy of eight. Compared with the face full of beard
(whiskers)
, the fallen teeth and wrinkled face of his lifetime, he seemed another person entirely. Had Wang not been his most intimate friend, knowing him
(familiar with him)
to the utmost, and moreover a childhood companion of the same village
(a friend of childhood)
, he would almost have failed to recognize him. For such beauty of bearing was something the layman had never possessed in all his life.
At the sight, Wang was overjoyed and astonished beyond measure; in his incoherence he asked abruptly
(abruptly)

: “Ah! So you have truly been reborn in the West! Otherwise, how could you have such a bearing? You yourself do not know that your face is now completely that of a tender, handsome boy. In life you lost more than half your teeth, and I once invited you to Songzhu Ju to have them set — do you still remember?” The layman said: “Yes, yes. I have come specially to tell you and report.” Wang said: “The West is a hundred thousand koṭis of Buddha-lands from here, no easy place to reach, yet you have actually arrived.” He answered: “My having attained it is entirely through the power of faith and vows.” Wang said: “How could you get here?” He answered: “Very easily — with a single thought one is there; in time you will know it yourself. When one wishes to come, one looks toward the darkness; when one wishes to go, one looks toward the brightness; that is all.” Wang asked again: “Have you seen the Buddha?” He answered: “Not yet.” “Why could you not see him?” “My meritorious practice is too shallow; I have not been born into the pond of seven jewels.” “If not born into the pond of seven jewels, where were you born?” The layman sighed deeply: “Alas, the place where I was born is merely the ground of the West. Ah, I suppose it counts as the borderland.”

The conversation was not yet finished when he suddenly awoke. Opening his eyes and recalling, he felt that the layman's words, bearing, radiance, and marks were vivid before his eyes, utterly unlike any inverted dream. He rose and looked at the clock; it was just past five in the afternoon. After a month
(after a month)

, with the year ending and spring returning, Wang happened to meet Wang Nengzhi, a kinsman by marriage of the layman. The latter, at their first meeting, said abruptly to Wang: “How strange! Last winter Zhu Xingwu came several times to converse with me, saying he had attained the borderland of the West and had come specially to report. I have long wished to visit you and tell you all this.” Wang then eagerly
(eagerly)

inquired what he had said, and Nengzhi related: “The moment I saw him, I asked: where have you been these past few months, and why did you not come sooner? The layman answered: I was detained in the realm of darkness for a long while on some matter; it was by the grace of Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva, who sent someone to escort me, that I could take the time to come. He also said: when I was alive, I gave you books on Buddha-recitation — have you practiced according to them? You once ran a restaurant and killed many creatures; your offenses are too heavy. From now on, besides striving in Buddha-recitation, you must repent all the more, and must take up a vegetarian diet and strictly abstain from killing. Rebirth in the West is the portion of every person, and it is very easy; by no means give up on yourself. I deeply regret having taken up Buddha-recitation so late and that my meritorious practice is so poor; you should enter into practice early as the essential thing — and so on.” After the layman's report, Wang's friends, hearing of it, mostly urged him to record it and publish it, to awaken people's faith. Wang therefore wrote it out plainly according to the facts, and appended to the manuscript a postscript: “I solemnly vow by the precepts that there is not a single false word, and that I have not added or subtracted a single word of Layman Zhu's replies in the dream.” Yesterday he sent the manuscript to this journal by swift letter, asking for its publication, and it is now published to inform the monastics and laypeople of the whole land.
Honghua Monthly
July
An
Gui

blocks.text: The Effortless Rebirth of Layman Wei Guoxing

inline.s: Feeling the fleeting shadow of each inch of declining time, / dreading that the store of future merit is not yet amassed; / purifying the heart in the Dharma Hall, / adjusting the robe and facing the pure, / forgetful of sleep past midnight, / diligent from dawn till dusk.” This Master Huiyuan of Mount Lu pronounced; and such did Layman Guoxing of western Shu put into practice.
On March 7, 2003
the fifth day
of the second month
of the lunar calendar),

around Focheng Temple in Qingyi Township, Mianyang City, Sichuan Province, auspicious clouds gathered into a canopy, a gentle breeze wafted peacefully, sacred birds sang, and rare incense scented the air. At exactly noon, faint heavenly music was heard as the clouds parted like scattered blossoms. Within the temple, monks and laity gathered in a crowd and recited the Buddha's name in unison. Amitābha Buddha, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva, and the pure and oceanlike assembly of Bodhisattvas, treading upon a thousand-petaled lotus, assembled in the sky above the Buddha Hall. More than three hundred people witnessed the Buddha with their own eyes; their emotion was uncontrollable, and weeping rose and fell in waves. Layman Wei Guoxing ascended the golden lotus platform and, amid the company of the Buddha and the host of Bodhisattvas, passed blissfully onward to the West, exactly as he had wished.
Layman Wei Guoxing was born on May 4, 1927
the fourth day
of the fourth month
of the lunar calendar),
in Xinglong Village, Third Cooperative, Qingyi Township, Mianyang City, Sichuan Province. Honest and sincere by nature, he made his living as a carpenter, and

he took refuge and received the precepts at Shengshui Temple. Deeply devoted to the Pure Land, he gave himself heart and soul to mindfulness of the Buddha, resolved with one mind to seek rebirth in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss. Toward the Buddha's teachings he was reverent and respectful to the utmost; he never declined to do a good deed because it was small, nor engage in an evil one because it was small. Every wholesome undertaking — releasing living beings, printing sutras, giving charity, assisting at deathbed recitation, and supporting temples — he always strove to perform to the measure of his ability.

In 2002 he fell ill with esophageal cancer, and all the more diligently did he recite the Buddha's name. He said that for one who recites the Buddha's name, the appearance of karmic hindrances is a case of a heavy offense being repaid lightly, and a test from the Buddha and the Bodhisattvas, so that one's rebirth at the end of life might be unobstructed. His family wished to send him to hospital for treatment, but he firmly declined, saying, “If I am to be hospitalized, let it be in the great hospital of Amitābha Buddha.” On this matter he asked the counsel of his master. Master Dexin instructed him: “At such a time you should redouble your efforts beyond ordinary measure. All the more concentrate your single mind and vigorously recite the Buddha's name; let go entirely of body and mind, and with utmost sincerity and earnestness seek rebirth as the essential matter. If your allotted years remain, the illness will heal of itself and create a wonder; if your allotted years are exhausted, then it is the time of your rebirth. At the very least you should strive to know the hour of your coming and, welcoming the Buddha's guidance, set an example for practitioners of recitation in later generations, and create a still greater wonder, benefiting countless sentient beings.” Hearing the master's instruction, his mind indeed opened and his understanding was freed, and he smiled radiantly. Before the Buddha he vowed to make the suffering of his illness a strengthening condition for his recitation and aspiration for rebirth, to let go utterly of his whole body and mind and the world, and to recite the Buddha's name with a wholly reverent heart, single-mindedly seeking rebirth in the Lotus Land.
One day he finally found Master Dexin and said, “Master, I have a joyful matter to tell you.”
What joyful matter?” asked Master Dexin.
He said, “While I was reciting the Buddha's name, the Buddha and the Bodhisattvas told me that in a few days they would come to take me to be reborn in the Western Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss.”

This was truly astonishing! How extraordinary! Hearing him say this, Master Dexin was filled with joy and exultation, and said to him with great earnestness, “Since you have attained such depth of practice and have received the Buddha's own prophecy, we should hold a seven-day recitation dharma assembly for your rebirth, to serve as a farewell with supportive chanting. On the day of the assembly you may follow Amitābha Buddha, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, and Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva and be reborn in perfect freedom. You set the time.”
Then let it be the twenty-ninth.”
Good, then it is agreed!”
The assembly began on the twenty-ninth day of the first lunar month and concluded on the fifth day of the second lunar month, lasting exactly seven days.

On the day the assembly was fulfilled, he said to everyone, “I must bring this assembly to a perfect completion. Why? Because many suffering beings say: ‘You always say that studying the Buddha's Way is good — but where is the good

The good lies in freedom over birth and death. And where does that freedom lie? Let us look! I will do it right before your eyes. If I fall short in it, then those who study the Buddha's Way would be speaking falsely. Therefore, in completing this great undertaking of my practice of the Dharma, I am giving you a model to behold. These suffering beings are deluded and upside down — but reflect: the thirty-two marks, the eighty minor characteristics…”

On the day before his passing, he himself led the assembly to the edge of a stream to release living creatures, and together with them walked around the Buddha reciting and chanting. On the night before his passing, he spoke to the assembly, saying: “There are still eleven hours,” and after lowering his head to glance a while at the watch on his wrist, he went on: “I am a man who loves to renounce above all. Even when I went everywhere to spread the word, I too was renouncing; yet everyone was filled with doubt, doubting this very fact — just think of it, what on earth is this? If you do not believe me, then on the fifth day of this lunar month please come and see for yourselves. Some people say that this old man has lost his mind. I tell you, this is the truth. Let me report to you: why do I do this? People in this world, all of you must renounce (he uttered the word ‘renounce’ with a very heavy and earnest tone) before you can put on clothes, before you can take a bath, before you can even cut your toenails and leave (making a gesture of helplessly letting go of the world). I deliberately want to do something that has a bit of form to it. Why? I deliberately want, while still alive, to stay here at Focheng, Qingyi Township, Mianyang City, for seven days. These seven days I am holding my seven-day recitation retreat here. Each day I join in reciting sutras, bowing in repentance, circumambulating the Buddha, and walking while reciting — but those who were told to come in are all coming on the twenty-ninth to bow to the Buddha, chant the sutras, and bow in repentance, because there are many who came merely out of curiosity and doubted the twenty-ninth I spoke of. As for this rebirth dharma assembly of my practice ground, at the opening ceremony on the first day — the afternoon of the twenty-eighth — the president of the Sichuan Buddhist Association gave the opening address (he lowered his head and looked at his watch), and tomorrow, the fifth, in the afternoon the closing ceremony of the rebirth dharma assembly will be held to conclude it. I hope you all will not regard this practice ground as superstition, or as some sort of scheme, or as ghosts and spirits, or as some Falun Gong organization stirring up trouble at this place. You who recklessly talk nonsense and take Buddhism for superstition — Buddhism is education; it educates people to walk the right path, the road of prosperity. These people teach you to do no evil and to practice all good, to be filial to your parents, and to take filial piety, brotherly respect, loyalty, and trustworthiness as the foundation. Of all virtues, filial piety is first; of all evils, lust is foremost. And now in this society everything has been turned into places of entertainment…”

At ten o'clock on the morning of the fifth day of the second lunar month, with two hours still to go before Layman Wei's passing, he held a farewell ceremony together with the more than fifteen hundred lay practitioners present and those who had come to watch the spectacle. The venerable elder bowed and offered incense before the Buddha in the great hall with calm composure, and finally gave an instruction to the assembly: “Venerable ones, good and wise friends, fellow practitioners, honored guests, and good people all — today is the day of my passing, and the seven-day recitation dharma assembly for rebirth has come to a perfect and successful conclusion. On this last day of parting, I thank you all for your care!” At that moment everyone was deeply stirred, overcome with a mingled grief and joy.

Thereupon Master Dexin, together with Layman Wei's family and the monastic and lay assembly, escorted him slowly into the Rebirth Hall of the lay practitioners' building. Before the Buddha, with utmost reverence, he prostrated and offered incense, then sat upright on a wooden chair, his hands forming the Amitābha mudra, and chanted the Buddha's name aloud with the assembly. Suddenly auspicious light entered the room, and a rare fragrance and sublime music arose — all who saw and heard it felt at once a peace of body and mind. When they looked again, Layman Wei Guoxing had already passed calmly away in the Buddha's presence. Freedom over birth and death — a song sung for a thousand ages; the art of reciting the Buddha's name at its utmost peak. From ancient times, masters of the Chan school and the teaching schools have stood dense as a forest in their great attainments; those who have transcended birth and death, left the dust, and been freed from the wheel of suffering, and who have done so as they willed, have never gone beyond this summit.

In lay life, Layman Wei Guoxing was but a carpenter, no man of high intellect or uncommon gifts; in a mere three or five years he recited the Buddha's name and was reborn in the Buddha-land — an attainment without precedent and beyond compare, enough to move heaven and earth and make spirits weep. From this it is fully proven that the words of the Buddha and the patriarchs are not false: whether the simple man or the simple woman, the wise or the virtuous, if one but gives rise to heartfelt faith and vows, and with all one's heart recites the Buddha's name seeking rebirth, all attain it equally — of a myriad who practice, a myriad go. Master Yinguang said: “One should give rise to a resolute, earnest vow: may I be freed from the suffering of the Saha world, may I obtain the bliss of the Pure Land. The urgency of this vow should be like one who has fallen into a latrine pit desperately seeking to get out, or like one bound in prison longing for home; since one's own strength cannot free one, one must beg someone of great power to pull one out.” He also said: “A single ‘Namo Amitābha Buddha’ — once you have recited it to the point of familiarity, there is still abundant power left over to become a Buddha! What regret is there in not studying other methods?” May all beings know that the light of life is as fleeting as lightning, and be wary of the dangers of the wheel of transmigration; hold fast to the name and recite the Buddha, and attain success in this very life. Namo Amitābha Buddha! Namo Amitābha Buddha! Namo Amitābha Buddha! “Unify the six faculties, and let the pure thought continue without break — this is foremost” indeed!
Recorded by Dharma Master Zhixing

blocks.text: On the Practice of Assisting the Dying toward Rebirth

inline.s: In this life, the suffering of illness is the hardest of all to bear. When illness leads to death, the pain is all the more bitter. At such a moment, if the assisting recitation is done effectively, one can turn thoughts of suffering into right mindfulness and, by virtue of the power of that vow, attain rebirth. Yet there are many different ways of assisting recitation, and unless they come from tested experience, some may even disturb the dying so that they cannot attain rebirth — this must be regarded with deep care. I recently met Dharma Master Tonghui and spoke with him about the method of assisting recitation. According to his practical experience, two points are most essential, and I record them as follows.

1. Whenever one accompanies a dying patient toward rebirth, there should be at least three people to a group. The voice should be clear and distinct, not too loud, so as not to disturb the patient. At first recite the six-syllable name (Namo Amituofo); when the patient is at the point of crisis, one should change to the four-syllable name (Amituofo), so that although the patient's strength is slight he can still follow — with six syllables his breath would fail. If the patient has already ceased breathing, change back to the six-syllable Buddha-name and continue until the recitation is brought to a complete conclusion.

2. If the patient senses that he is being harassed by demons, and suffers so that he can hardly bear it, continuing for days without relief, one should then invite three people who can recite the Śūraṅgama Mantra to recite it together, at least three times. By virtue of that mantra's power the evil demons will depart far away, the patient will be free of suffering, and he can then lift up right mindfulness and be reborn in the West.

May this merit adorn the Buddha's Pure Land; / Above, may it repay the fourfold graciousness; / Below, may it relieve the three paths of suffering. / May all who see and hear this / Awaken the bodhi mind; / When this body of retribution is ended, / May we together be reborn in the Land of Bliss!
Namo Amitābha Buddha
Namo Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva
Namo Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva
